meta.title: A sufficiently detailed spec is code
meta.author: Gabriella439

comments.author: amw-zero
comments.text:

comments.author: davmac
comments.text:
Asserting that a prime number generator always generates a prime number is likely more difficult than producing prime numbers


This seems to me to be a misunderstanding of what "asserting" means. An assertion is just a claim or proposition; making an assertion is trivial (the only potential difficulty comes from expressing it, but "always generates a prime number" isn't difficult to express). Assertion is not the same as verification.

comments.author: amw-zero
comments.text: That's why I asked what OP meant. I really wish OP would reply instead of people talking on their behalf.

comments.author: hyperpape
comments.text:
Not OP, of course, but it's very intuitive to me: stating properties your system must have is often easier than writing a program that has those properties. Note: I agree that validating that the system has those properties is usually harder than either. As a matter of language, to "assert X" is not to "verify X". I assert that this is true, but leave the verification to someone who wants to consult a dictionary.

For instance:


any sequence of steps in a traveling salesman optimization should transform a cycle into a new cycle[0]

the program must never dereference a null pointer

any sequence of method calls to the public API must return a value in finite time


In general, most programming languages have limited functionality for quantification or higher order statements about code (not to be confused with higher order functions). It's easy to build a Foobut you can't easily express the predicate "there exists a Foo" or say that "all Foos are Bars".

A bit of speculation: unlike an awful lot of people in this field, I came to programming as an adult, after I knew formal logic and philosophy, and some abstract math. Code has some amazing properties, but the idea that it has any privileged place in specifying ideas is very foreign to me. I wonder if those two facts are connected.

[0] In a sense, lots of heuristic optimizations work by taking a cycle, breaking it, and reforging the cycle. You can either look at that as a series of steps where every so many steps you recreate a cycle, or you can treat the breakings and rejoinings as parts of single steps that transform one cycle into another according to pattern. The former perspective it what the code forces you to do, and it is a colossal pain in the ass.

comments.author: muvlon
comments.text: In a design process, assertions compose trivially - just assert all of them. Sure, you might get an unsatisfiable set of assertions, but that's the only failure mode. Implementation details can be incompatible with each other in arbitrarily complex ways.

comments.author: davmac
comments.text:
"Assert" does not mean "verify". A specification can require (assert) some condition (property) but not specify how that condition should be satisfied. (Verification on the other hand is an action on the implementation, not the spec).

For example: "the numbers should be output in order, lowest to highest" as an assertion in a specification does not specify a sorting algorithm. This is a trivial example since we all probably have a handle on some sorting algorithms and such a requirement wouldn't give us any pause, but it's certainly possible to have more complicated requirements with less obvious solutions. And even with the sorting example, there are numerous different algorithms that could be chosen that would satisfy the spec.

So: no, a sufficiently detailed spec is not necessarily code (notwithstanding that "sufficiently detailed" is perhaps ambiguous).

comments.author: bakkot
comments.text:
An example: the JavaScript specification is very detailed, to the point that there are multiple projects (ecmaspeak, esmeta) which attempt to derive a fully executable JavaScript interpreter from just the specification. And they kind of work! We've gone to a great deal of effort to make the spec clear and consistent, and indeed it strongly resembles code most of the time.

But. The specification leaves the hard parts of a production JS implementation completely unspecified. For example, it says nothing whatsoever about how to implement garbage collection. And while there is a detailed (and formally verified) memory model for SharedArrayBuffers, you are left completely on your own as to how to actually implement shared-memory multithreading in a manner consistent with the memory model. Even Maps and Sets are specified as a simple list of key-value pairs (but the spec requires you to have sub-linear performance for various operations, so you must use a different implementation).

In our case, I think it is correct to say that the specification is simpler than the corresponding code, at least when speaking of production engines like V8. But it is also true that you cannot get remotely close to deriving a production engine merely from the specification.

comments.author: rs86
comments.text: JS is not the best here. This works well enough for a formally specified language. Scheme, ADA, Standard ML have formal specs that define this much better than JS. The dynamic typing story in JS is hell for static analysis.

comments.author: andyc
comments.text:
I don't think what you wrote is very relevant to the parent comment

Scheme and Standard ML likely share the same property mentioned -- their spec doesn't say anything about garbage collection.

That alone makes the implementation longer than the spec.

I don't think Scheme and Standard ML have threads either, so they don't have an analogue of the SharedArrayBuffer issue


I think you are conflating two issues:  the language design of JavaScript, and the quality of the spec (and its length with compared with the length of an implementation)

comments.author: marginalia
comments.text:
The funny part is that a big reason we have programming languages is that logicians found spoken language too ambiguous, and invented tools such as syllogistic logic, then symbolic logic, and so on as a pry bar for humans to be able to think and speak more correctly without stumbling on the inherent limitations in spoken language[1][2].

Then computers came along and we realized they could work in this paradigm even better than humans could.  In many ways, the notion of programming in spoken language is a regression to a pre-socratic level of understanding of language and logic.

Legalese has somewhat analogous roots, but has come about from the need to defend against adversarial misinterpretations.

[1] Time flies like an arrow, fruit flies like a banana.

[2] All feathers are light, therefore no feathers are dark.  But a contradicton!  This feather is black, therefore some feathers are not light, therefore some feathers are heavy.

comments.author: etler
comments.text:
I've experienced this first hand. To validate the concept of a project I'm working on I developed a detailed spec of the behavior fleshed out with the help of AI. I used that spec as a guide to have an agent build a proof of concept for me. After having cleaned up the codebase from what it produced, the resulting code is actually shorter than the spec! And of course the process of actually implementing it exposed many areas of the spec that were ambiguous and needed correcting.

You simply cannot predict the final shape of a project up front. You need to experiment and get your hands dirty and try different approaches, and the only way to do that properly with enough fidelity to ensure you are actually building the right thing is to read and understand the code.

AI is incredibly effective at accelerating what you do. It helped me do research, it helped me spec it out and figure out a lot of edge cases ahead of time, it helped me prototype it, it helped me test it, it helped me iterate on it, and it helped me refactor it.

But I absolutely could not stop at the spec level and expect it to produce a result that was remotely adequate for the project.

Where I don't quite agree with the author is this:


Specifications were never meant to be time-saving devices. If you are optimizing for delivery time then you are likely better off authoring the code directly rather than going through an intermediate specification document.


Working with a spec was absolutely a time saving device, but not in terms of saving time producing the final result, but rather saving time by not wasting time building the wrong thing.

A specification is by definition an approximation, and very rarely do we have a fully fleshed out vision of what to build in our heads before we build it. By approximating a problem we can quickly iterate on it and simulate the complete project through a lower fidelity mockup. Simply working on the specification saved me time by exposing issues that I did not think of at a high level. Then, having AI produce a rough proof of concept helped surface which areas needed the most work, and which concepts did not work as elegantly as I had hoped ahead of time. AI was able to handle the easier parts well so I could focus my attention on the hardest parts.


More generally, the principle of "garbage in, garbage out" applies here. There is no world where you input a document lacking clarity and detail and get a coding agent to reliably fill in that missing clarity and detail. Coding agents are not mind readers and even if they were there isn't much they can do if your own thoughts are confused.


This is absolutely correct, however I think it's missing the bigger picture which is that sometimes the hardest part of a project is finding the garbage. Working with AI exposed the limits of my understanding of my own project much faster than if I were to do an earnest attempt by hand. Even where the AI made stupid assumptions, it still exposed areas of my specification and understanding that were not fully thought out. Agents are indeed not mind readers, but the practice of asking them to try has been the most effective way for me to recognize where my own thoughts are confused.

I think the overarching message is correct here. AI cannot build something for you when you don't know in minute detail what you want, but I think the continuation of that thought is that AI exposes where you don't know what you want and iterating with AI is very powerful for refining your ideas quickly.

comments.text: This resonates with me. And although slightly tangential, it serves as an anecdote of where I've personally landed in "top-down versus bottom-up": ideal software design is a combination/interplay of the two (not a "versus").

comments.author: qznc
comments.text:
A spec describe all possible implementations. The concrete code is just one of them. Thus, if your spec is your code, then the spec is probably overly restrictive.

The spec might or might not be simpler/shorter than the code. That probably depends mostly on the APIs available for the implementation.

comments.author: ptman
comments.text: I'm in hard agreement. I've heard lots of variations of "just commit the spec/usecases". Compilers are deterministic. We've spent 10-20 years working on software reproducability. It has value. Producing code from spec isn't reproducible. It isn't meant to be reproducible. But you really want to have the source code as a source of truth that you can deterministically convert to a working binary.

comments.author: tuxes
comments.text:
Some code is overfit:


the exact decomposition of the problem into functions/types.

the exact naming of variables.

the choice of libraries

the exact text used in UIs/comments/error messages

which unit tests happen to be implemented, or not

the implementation of a function: should we use foreach, for, do...while, map, ...

the path taken, e.g. the order of commits

the programming language


All of those are important, as we all know, for various reasons.

But how important are they, relative to their cost in having a human decide?

That gap is the opportunity that is being exploited by the LLM agents.

So the question becomes come back to the title: sufficiently detailed... for what?

comments.author: amw-zero
comments.text:
Very thoughtful post, though I respectfully disagree with the main premise.

As far as measurable evidence of my disagreement, there is still a large gap between the spec here and the implementation. I ran cloc on the repo, and there's 3,388 lines of Markdown to 16,063 lines of Elixir. So it's not like the generated code is a 1:1 mapping of the Markdown spec.

As far as my philosophical position, which to be clear I'm biased in because I'm heavily in favor of specification:

Specifications are necessary, and are sorely missed in our industry. Djikstra himself was a proponent of specification. And I quote:


It is our position that a solid product consists of a triple: a program, a functional specification, and a proof that the program meets the functional specification.



EWD 1060


So, there must be some separation of the code from its specification, else we can't ever make a statement about the code's correctness. We can debate what those specifications look like (how much or how little detail they should reference, whether or not they're Hoare-logic style or refinement style, etc.), but we can't just say "the code is the code, and that's it."

Now, it's a very valid question as to whether or not an AI prompt counts as a specification. I actually don't think it does! So maybe we're in agreement there. I'm more fond of executable specifications, e.g. as produced in a language like Quint. An LLM can help you create such specifications, but since they're used as tools for verification I think you should spend extra care validating the specs themselves, manually.

comments.author: rs86
comments.text: Prose specs are not specs… you can’t check what they specify. On the other hand a formal spec can nicely expand to hundreds of times the original code.

comments.author: zdsmith
comments.text:
There is… well, I can’t say there’s a way out of this. But there are approaches that can make it more effective than what the Symphony team did.

There are a couple truths about coding agents that come into play:


They’re very good at structured text and very good with any kind of compiler or linter that gives them actionable feedback.

They don’t need to be used as mechanical text generation tools—“make a spec out of this codebase”; they can also be instructed to ask the user useful questions.


I’ve got my own formal specification language, and it’s got a skill for coding agents to write it.

The skill explains the syntax and semantics of the language, but just as critically, it instructs the agent not to simply write the spec; rather, the agent guides the user through the process of thinking rigorously and unambiguously about the program that they want to specify. It proposes possible entities and framings but asks the user to consider them and decide on the approach. The code is there; sometimes when I’m in this process I say “I don’t know; read the code”. But the purpose, first of all, is that I ought to understand the core concepts and models at work better than I did.

And: it’s a formal method, with a model checker, so it’s a meaningful document. The agent can check the document and correct under specifications, contradictions, etc - including those that arose from my faulty misunderstanding.

This is no magic bullet… in particular, would I claim that Claude Code can simply reimplement a program from a spec? Not yet, that’s for sure. But it’s definitely helpful; already it gives the agent a quasi objective standard to compare its implementation against.

The precise use of these things in agent assisted development is experimental. But! I can claim more confidently that agents can help write useful, correct, meaningful specs to a much better extent than “rewrite this program as prose.”

(The language in question: https://pantagruel-language.com/)

comments.author: lamg
comments.text: Interesting. Seems a less optimistic version of this https://structuredprogramming.substack.com/p/the-new-generation-of-programming

comments.author: chriswarbo
comments.text:
I think the idea of specifying everything up-front is the hard part. When a human interacts with an LLM, they can correct the mistakes it makes, then have it carry on.

Running an LLM without a human in the loop is giving up that feedback channel. Attempts to specify all instructions up-front are trying to anticipate EVERY POSSIBLE mistake, whether it would actually happen or not. It's a much harder problem; and, as TFA says, usually ends up isomorphic to writing the code ourselves.
